articles.title_orig: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
articles.title_zh: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
articles.content_orig:
Xbox VP of Next Generation Jason Ronald has clarified that Project Helix is "designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games, not a PC that can also play console games."
In the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine , Ronald described Project Helix as "the ultimate gaming machine – one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed."
"The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Project Helix's console and PC compatibility in March, adding that the console will "lead in performance" for Xbox and PC games.
As Ronald previously discussed at GDC Festival of Gaming , Project Helix will utilise neural rendering, which uses AI models to enhance graphics. Ronald identified neural rendering as a particular focus for Project Helix, as it also addresses the ongoing component crisis.
"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and platform designer, it's one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also [making] things accessible and affordable."
"This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower [and] additional memory."
He concluded: "I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last ten years."
Reports last month indicated that Project Helix is expected to launch during the 2028 holiday season , with a projected price between $1,200 and $1,800.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.
The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.
Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.
Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. When markets opened in the United States, tech stocks mostly stabilized from a sell-off the day before, with the Nasdaq index starting the day flat. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.

articles.title_orig: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow? : Planet Money
articles.title_zh: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow? : Planet Money
articles.content_orig:
A cash cow. Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac hide caption
Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?
Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money . By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
Then Google vice president of search Marissa Mayer in 2009. ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion . That's more than a millionfold increase.
Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.
In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.
Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer , a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.
Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."
Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.
If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.
Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.
The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail .
Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.
The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.
Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?
Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages , recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go .
The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.
But they didn't release it.
Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.
Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.
So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?
Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?
His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.
In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.
Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.
"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.
Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist , sexist , and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.
And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.
Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma . Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.
Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.
We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?
Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.
The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.

articles.title_orig: Well-known journalist who reported death threats is gunned down on street in Costa Rica
articles.title_zh: Well-known journalist who reported death threats is gunned down on street in Costa Rica
articles.content_orig:
Costa Rican independent journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who had called out alleged ties between drug traffickers and politicians on social media, was shot dead Monday outside the capital San Jose, authorities said.
Two men riding on a motorcycle opened fire on Rodriguez as he was driving through the town of Santo Domingo de Heredia, police chief Raul Rivera said. Rodriguez was attacked at around 3:20 p.m. local time amid heavy traffic on a main highway, Reuters reported , citing the Red Cross.
Rodriguez, 50, had reported receiving several death threats from drug trafficking groups.
He would name drug lords by their full names and claimed to have provided reports to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration regarding links between drug traffickers and powerful figures in politics and business.
When President Laura Fernandez was running for office last year, she sued Rodriguez for defamation after he posted a video claiming her home had been built with money allegedly provided by a drug trafficker.
"Regardless of the content of his statements, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression," Fernandez said in a video released by her office .
Rodriguez ran for president in 2022, but his nomination was rejected by electoral authorities on technical grounds.
He also accused his ex-wife of being involved in drug trafficking. She has filed a complaint alleging he sexually abused their children.
The Costa Rican Journalists' Association condemned his killing and demanded "a swift investigation."
"All evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica -- a person who published information about organized crime in the country," the association's president, Yanancy Noguera, told AFP.
In recent years, Costa Rica has gone from being a drug transit point to a logistics hub for trafficking, and has lost its status as one of the safest countries in Central America.
Fernandez, who took office in May, campaigned on a promise to crack down on the crime wave, and said she is drawing inspiration from El Salvador's iron-fisted President Nayib Bukele.
Fernandez herself that she has received intelligence reports showing that jailed gang members have ordered her assassination, the Tico Times reported on Monday.
Attorney General Carlo Diaz announced an investigation into the murder, adding that Rodriguez -- who had contributed to various Costan Rican print, radio and television media outlets and more recently turned to social media -- had declined to enter a witness protection program.
Diaz told local media the crime scene resembled a contract killing, Reuters reported.
"We know he was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking," Diaz said. "Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society."
According to Reporters Without Borders , more than half of the world's countries now fall into the "difficult" or "very serious" categories for press freedom.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft testing Remote Lock for lost or stolen Windows devices
articles.title_zh: Microsoft testing Remote Lock for lost or stolen Windows devices
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them.
Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta ( Build 26320.10003 ) and Experimental ( Build 26340.10013 ) channels.
Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro.
After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked.
"Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines . "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."
Admins can lock a device from the Intune admin center using the following procedure:

articles.title_orig: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

articles.content_orig:
Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic
Images show part of the bridge destroyed
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike on Kerch bridge an 'unprecedented operation'
Russia also struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said
The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
European regulators warn that a nationwide blackout could create cooling problems at several Ukrainian reactors simultaneously. How realistic is that scenario, and how well prepared are the plants?
Hungary 's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said that rail traffic was being suspended to and from Ukraine on Tuesday and Wednesday, after a Russian drone came down in Western Ukraine.
"A Russian drone recently crashed in Zakarpattia, ‌300 metres from the Mukachevo railway station. The ‌Hungarian ​crew of a train arriving from Hungary was ordered to disembark," Magyar said in a Facebook post.
"We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for ​today and tomorrow," Magyar said.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban had earlier said that Russian drones had attacked Zakarpattia, targeting areas near Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, not far from the border area with Hungary.
"As Russia intensifies ‌its attacks on Ukraine's civilian population, similar operations against Zakarpattia, which until now has ​been relatively protected ⁠due to its geographical location, can also be expected in ⁠the future," ​she said.
Russia state media has reported that President Vladimir Putin has been briefed by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin "on the situation around the Crimean Bridge," citing Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
"Following the government commission meeting, Marat Khusnullin reported to President Putin on the situation surrounding the Crimean Bridge," Peskov told reporters.
"According to the Investigative Committee, on November 16 and 17, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the Crimean Bridge using unmanned aerial vehicle, resulting in damage to the structure," TASS reported.
Russian media also quoted Peskov as saying that the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia would be "even better" after it was restored, giving an indication as to the extent of the damage caused.
"There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before," Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that the Kerch bridge was targeted by Ukrainian forces, describing it as "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure."
"Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea," Zelenskyy said in a lengthy post on social media platform X.
The Ukrainian leader said the strike was a culmination of an operation "carried out over several weeks" by his country's military and involved destroying air defense systems, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment in the lead up to the attack.
Zelenskyy said that the road section of the bridge was hit by "Palianytsia" drones and while the railway section was targeted by "Neptune" missiles and "Ruta" drones.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," Zelenskyy said and pointed to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure.
His post was accompanied by footage appearing to show the moment the bridge was struck and then the subsequent aftermath with one part of the bridge collapsed.
Germany and Norway will fund a new US air defense package for Ukraine's defensive needs, according to Germany's defense chief.
"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.
Pistorius said that Germany would contribute $300 million (€272 million) towards the weapons package that would include Patriot interceptor missiles.
The package will also include previously announced IRIS-T systems, as well as new radars and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets and drones.
The announcement comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later today.
Germany has, since the start of Russia's invasion, provided civilian aid totalling more than €45.7 billion and provided or earmarked military aid of around €57.8 billion, according to the German government .
Ukraine 's Deputy Energy ​Minister Artem Nekrasov, said that Russian strikes on energy infrastructure had caused power outages in nine Ukrainian regions.
"As a result of the strikes, some consumers have been left without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Chernihiv and Chernivtsi regions," Nekrasov said.
"The situation is extremely difficult ⁠in ​the Dnipropetrovsk and ​Zaporizhzhia regions. Since ​last ‌week, Russia has been continuously ​attacking ⁠energy facilities in the ⁠Dnipro ​region," Nekrasov said.

A government meeting is expected to take place soon following the strike on the Kerch bridge, Russian state media agency TASS reported.
"A meeting of the government commission on the aftermath of the attack on the Crimean Bridge, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, will be held soon at Government House," TASS quoted the Russian government as saying.
"The meeting will address issues related to the restoration of the Crimean Bridge and the organization of transport links," TASS reported.
The extent of the damage caused is not yet known and Russian officials have only confirmed that a strike had taken place and that traffic has been disrupted.
A drone strike on Crimea has killed two people, according to the Russia-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov.
He said on Telegram that the strike took place in the Leninsky district of Crimea, which was seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Earlier Aksyonov said that Ukraine had struck the Kerch bridge, causing traffic to be suspended.
Moscow built the Kerch Bridge to link the annexed Crimean Peninsula to the Russian region of Krasnodar Krai in the northern Caucasus.
The route is a major source of supplies for Russian forces in Ukraine's occupied Kherson region and is a strategically significant target for Ukrainian forces.
The Kerch bridge, which links the occupied Crimean peninsula to mainland Russia , has been partially destroyed, according to unofficial reports.
Photos on various Telegram channels appear to show that one of the arches and part of the roadway have collapsed following a strike.
Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski shared a picture on his X account showing a single arch where there should be two, simply exclaiming "Wow."
Reports on the extent of damage have yet to be confirmed by official sources, but images and videos of the bridge are being widely circulated in the Ukrainian media space.
Russia's Transport Ministry said there had been an overnight drone strike on November 17 leading to a temporary suspension of traffic. It advised motorists not to travel towards the bridge and wait for further information.
Ukraine's national police said late Monday that the death toll from a Russian strike on a village in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia earlier this month had risen to 72.
Four people were still missing after authorities concluded a two-week search operation on Monday.
Russia hit a former school that was used as an aid distribution center in Komyshuvakha on November 2 as people were collecting humanitarian supplies. The attack was one of the deadliest of the war.
The village is located close to the frontline.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

Home Depot ( HD ) is rebuilding its C-suite ahead of the new year.
The home improvement retailer said Tuesday that CFO Richard McPhail will slide into the CEO role on Nov. 23. He will be the company's seventh CEO in a history that began with Arthur Blank and Bernie Marcus as co-founders in 1978.
Current CEO Ted Decker will transition to the chairman of the board role.
McPhail takes the leadership baton at HD amid the backdrop of a US housing market he has called "frozen" in the recent past.
"First of all, our customers are the homeowner — and so they're one of the most resilient customer cohorts in the economy," McPhail told Yahoo Finance in a February 2026 interview. "But they're feeling pressure like everyone else. They tell us they have concerns around housing affordability, general affordability, and broader concerns over uncertainty and job loss. So there is pressure on the market. If you look at housing turnover, that's actually been frozen for three years; we have been at historical lows in housing turnover for three years in a row."
Here's what we know about McPhail:
He has spent more than 21 years at Home Depot.
He has held the CFO role for more than seven years and also leads the "Pro Acceleration" office, which is focused on improving services for professional Home Depot shoppers.
He started his career in 1996 as an investment banking associate specializing in private equity and M&A at Wachovia Securities. He moved to the corporate finance function at Arthur Anderson in 1998.
He moved to London for five years to work at Marconi Corp in corporate finance.
He is a graduate of Duke University (MBA) and North Carolina State University (BA)
He is known to be a golf and fishing fan.

articles.title_orig: "Essentially Worthless" - Disgruntled Fans Are Review Bombing Pikmin 4 On Switch 2
articles.title_zh: "Essentially Worthless" - Disgruntled Fans Are Review Bombing Pikmin 4 On Switch 2
articles.content_orig:
So far, the Nintendo Switch 2 upgraded editions of games originally released on the Switch have been a bit of a mixed bag. While games like Kirby and the Forgotten Land received significant new content and noticeable performance upgrades, others such as Xenoblade Chronicles X weren’t quite as well received. According to many Pikmin fans, the recently released Switch 2 version of Pikmin 4 falls into the latter camp.
Pikmin 4: Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is an upgrade for the 2023 Switch game with added levels and higher-resolution graphics. It came out last Thursday and costs $10 to upgrade from the original Nintendo Switch version. Unfortunately, the new version of Pikmin 4 currently has a dismal 1.9 out of 10 user score on Metacritic, a massive drop from the original version’s 8.9 user rating .
As for why it’s drawing so much ire, user reviews claim the Switch 2 version runs worse than it did on the previous system. Multiple players cite frame rate drops alongside longer load times. “This is essentially a paid downgrade and calling this a ‘lazy Switch 2 Edition’ or a ‘waste of money’ is an understatement for what is supposed to be an upgrade,” a Metacritic user review from PrestonandTom reads. They go on to claim that standard load times have gone from “six seconds to 30+ seconds” and that the frame rate has gone from a “consistent 30 FPS to an inconsistent 30 FPS.”
“Actively makes the game worse,” a review from Kevosan corroborates. “Longer load times than on NS1, frame drops, and glitches. The new content is NOT worth the trade-off. Standards are in the depths with this one.” Beyond the technical issues, some players also aren’t happy with the added Dandori Academy levels, which are apparently repetitive and reuse areas from the main story.
Still, there are a few upgrades that even the biggest detractors are fine with. The Switch 2 version of Pikmin 4 runs at a higher resolution, and some users commented that the voice support, which lets you give voice commands to the weird little dog-alien Oatchi, is a nice addition.
Many on the Pikmin subreddit weren’t quite as up in arms over the new version of Pikmin 4 , with some saying that the negative reviews were being overdramatic. “0.6 is a score I’d only give to a game that is sub-functional,” one Redditor said about the review-bombed Metacritic page. Others argued that while the new Dandori Academy levels may reuse maps, the new enemy placements and other changes make these areas feel different.
Still, regardless of how fans feel about this upgrade, many Pikmin-heads are worried that the somewhat light changes compared to other Switch 2 editions mean that the series isn't being prioritized as highly as some of Nintendo's other tentpole releases. While Pikmin 5 hasn't been announced, at least the recently announced Pikmin shorts offer something to look forward to.

articles.title_orig: The new tax plan that could stop Social Security cuts
articles.title_zh: The new tax plan that could stop Social Security cuts
articles.content_orig:
Congress has six years to enact changes to Social Security to prevent cuts to retirement benefits. Senators elected in the Nov. 3 midterms will be in office when the deadline arrives, and their decisions may be critical in making tax changes that can affect Social Security.
During the midterm campaign season, tax policy surfaced in the debate over Social Security in two different ways. Many Democrats, and some Republicans, called for high earners to pay more in Social Security payroll taxes, while many Republicans touted a recently enacted tax deduction for adults 65 and older.
The diverging tactics come at a crucial moment for reform: The first could increase revenue flowing into the program. The second reduces eligible older adults' income taxes and can lower the taxes some beneficiaries pay on Social Security benefits, reducing program revenue.
Social Security trustees' latest projections show the trust fund used to pay retirement benefits may start to become depleted in 2032, when 78% of benefits would be payable.
Lawmakers do have some leeway — if the program's retirement and disability trust funds are combined, depletion would be pushed out to 2034, when 83% of scheduled benefits would be payable. But that's still a haircut for retirees — and it's coming soon.
"We've waited too long already, and the consequences are that the gap has grown larger," Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said of Social Security's shortfall.
On the campaign trail, midterm candidates largely avoided specifics on how they would reform Social Security. However, raising the payroll tax cap, also known as the taxable maximum, was a popular choice among Democratic candidates. That would require people who earn more than the cap, currently $184,500, to begin contributing payroll taxes for their earnings above that amount.
Meanwhile, some Republican candidates said they would extend the temporary senior tax deduction of up to $6,000 per eligible individual that is set to expire in 2028.
The deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in July of last year and billed as a senior bonus, was among the factors that moved Social Security trustees' retirement trust fund depletion projections three months sooner, according to an annual report released in June.
Here's what experts say could be in store now that Democrats have won control of the House and Senate.
Social Security is a pay-as-you-go system that relies on payroll taxes from workers to help make monthly benefit payments to millions of Americans.
In 2026, earnings up to $184,500 are subject to that tax. Workers and employers each contribute 6.2% of pay up to that threshold, while self-employed individuals pay 12.4%.
The wage cap will rise in 2027 to $192,300. It adjusts higher annually to reflect incremental changes in the average wage index.
On the campaign trail, some House and Senate candidates said the cap should be raised or eliminated entirely so high earners contribute more.
Following the election, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who is expected to become the next chair of the Social Security subcommittee, said on X on Nov. 7 that his proposal to increase benefits by at least $2,400 per year and "scrap the cap" on earnings subject to Social Security taxes would be a "top priority."
Outgoing Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., responded on X that the plan would "put a 12.4% tax" on people who are not millionaires or billionaires.
The idea of higher payroll taxes has broader support. A national survey fielded in February found most respondents — 79% — support raising taxes for wages over $400,000, according to the University of Maryland School of Public Policy. The change was the most popular option tested among the 2,509 adults surveyed.
Rising income inequality has meant the payroll tax cap no longer covers 90% of earnings, though that percentage was expected to remain constant when lawmakers enacted the last major reforms to the program in 1983, according to research from the Roosevelt Institute, a New York-based liberal think tank. The share of earnings covered by Social Security payroll taxes fell to around 83% in 2000 and has mostly stabilized at that level, according to the institute.
Despite candidates mentioning plans to change the cap during election season, some experts say Congress may put off tax hikes that could be politically unpopular.
"I think lawmakers may put some of these taxes on the table closer to 2032, when the Social Security trust fund hits insolvency," said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. "In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute."
If the payroll tax cap were lifted from just under $200,000 to $300,000 in earnings per year, that would cost someone at that higher income threshold about $6,700 more in direct payroll taxes, Riedl said.
"There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term," Riedl said. In the long term, though, "everything is on the table," she said.
While many Democrats have pushed for raising those taxes, some Republicans have also shared their openness to doing so.
"There's a crack in the dam there breaking," Dan Adcock, director of government relations and policy at the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, said of the Republican support.
Even if lawmakers raise or eliminate the cap, they would still need to agree on other changes to shore up the program. Republicans may want benefit cuts such as raising the retirement age in exchange for increasing taxes, Adcock said.
Just how far adjusting the taxable maximum would go to help solve Social Security's funding woes depends on how it is applied.
If the cap is eliminated starting in 2027, with the full 12.4% tax applying to all earnings and no benefit credit for earnings above the current threshold, that would eliminate 58% of the long-range actuarial balance over 75 years, according to a September analysis by the Social Security Administration.
Applying the 12.4% payroll tax rate to earnings over $250,000 starting in 2027 could address 57% of the long-range balance, according to the SSA, provided there are no benefit increases in exchange for the extra contributions.
If the 12.4% payroll tax rate were applied to earnings over $400,000 starting in 2027 without benefit increases, that would eliminate 53% of the long-range actuarial balance, the agency's analysis found.
Eventually, all earnings would be subject to Social Security payroll taxes as the gap between the taxable maximum, which increases every year, and the new threshold closes over time.
Yet some experts say raising the payroll tax cap could have consequences for taxpayers and the economy.
Raising the cap would be an "unprecedented increase" in marginal tax rates, according to William McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, an independent tax policy research organization.
Lifting the threshold could add more than 12 percentage points to the cost of earning an additional dollar of wages, McBride said. Those higher costs could affect the labor market, which may see higher unemployment as a result of the change, he said.
OBBBA's new senior tax deduction of up to $6,000 per individual — or "bonus additional amount for seniors," as it was dubbed in an early version of the legislation — is in effect for tax years 2025 through 2028.
Lawmakers elected to Congress in the midterms may decide whether to extend the temporary tax break.
"2028 is going to be a presidential election year, and I would not expect either party to be willing to allow any senior tax cuts to expire while they're competing for senior votes," Riedl said.
When President Donald Trump signed OBBBA into law in 2025, the White House said in a release: "No tax on Social Security is a reality." However, the new law does not eliminate taxes on Social Security benefits.

articles.title_orig: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
articles.title_zh: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue.
The Trump administration on Monday announced it was tightening a loophole that has allowed Chinese tech firms to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing the most advanced A.I. chips through third countries.
The move comes just days ahead of President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in the wake of Nvidia, the creator of the most advanced AI chips, becoming enmeshed in an international scandal that prompted the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang and a fresh round of scrutiny over the company’s ties to China.
The new rule released by the Commerce Department will require that buyers of advanced semiconductors from certain countries will need to secure a license to sell or transfer those chips.The administration said the rule would specifically impact buyers from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, describing those countries as having a “higher than normal” risk of evading current sanctions.
The measure is set to go into effect in 90 days.
China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia. Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports.
The new rule will also give Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wide discretion as to which chips may require more safeguards. According to the rules, the secretary may inform a company selling AI chips “orally” about stricter export rules on certain items if the department believes there is “an unacceptable risk.”
The rules came days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Lutnick for failing to properly oversee the chip exports to China in a CNBC interview on Sunday.
The rare public criticism came after Huang’s resignation as head of Nvidia in the wake of revelations about his extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected by the Commerce Department of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls, but a month-long investigation by the Commerce Department into Megaspeed was halted last year after a top Nvidia official intervened , according to the New York Times.
“Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said on CNBC on Sunday. “But Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
“President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage,” Bessent added.
Both Lutnick and Bessent are expected to travel with Trump to China this week, according to Semafor. Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Aside from AI chips, the first-of-its-kind summit will also focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons.
The federal government began restricting China's access to AI chips in Trump's first term, as both countries raced to become the leader  in this fast-evolving technology. The Biden administration intensified this policy , making the export of advanced chips to China illegal in 2022. Beijing nevertheless still succeeded in stockpiling thousands of chips to build its own AI systems thanks to an international smuggling network.
Last year, Trump reversed his own administration’s export restrictions, allowing Nvidia to sell two types of computer chip used in the development of artificial intelligence to "approved customers" in China in exchange for a portion of the revenue cut. Those moves are poised to draw more scrutiny next year when Democrats take control of Congress, with both chambers likely probing the Trump Administration's AI policies in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Congressional lawmakers have asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as a part of the investigation.

Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.title_zh: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.title_zh: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department on Monday tightened export restrictions designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips amid a dispute in the Trump administration over how to handle the issue.
The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes such as China, Iran and Russia.
The move comes as President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week, and on the heels of a scandal involving the chipmaking giant Nvidia, and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang, who has pushed for the ability to sell Nvidia chips abroad.
Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital affairs — including one he had with a Chinese woman who worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. The Commerce and Justice Departments began investigating Megaspeed, a major purchaser of Nvidia chips, in 2024 as part of a broader probe into an ecosystem of foreign companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, CNN has reported .
The Nvidia saga has put greater public scrutiny on the Commerce Department’s role in regulating the sale of crucial American technologies abroad. Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in a Situation Room meeting over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat.
The new rule is also a replacement for a Joe Biden-era export control rule that the Trump administration let lapse last year. Trump officials saw the Biden policy as an impediment to American businesses.
The Commerce Department had resisted putting the new rule into place for some time while other top officials in the Trump administration had been pushing for it, including Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, sources said.
That dynamic could be significant going forward because Commerce holds the tools of enforcement. Experts noted that the rule itself appeared to be strong but that the implementation would determine whether or not it has teeth.
The rule is “the first good-faith effort to actually close loopholes in export controls in a year and a half,” said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
With the Commerce Department announcement coming the same week that Trump is set to travel to China, administration officials are also bracing for a Chinese response, according to a senior administration official. But some expect that any response will come after Trump’s visit largely because China wants to avoid dramatic tension during the meeting, the official said.
At a press briefing on Tuesday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing “will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the new restrictions were “a typical case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction. It runs counter to the consensus reached by both sides.”
The Commerce Department noted that the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”
But as Trump left the White House on Monday on his way to Asia, he downplayed reported disagreements inside his administration on the matter and said he has no plans to fire Lutnick, who some officials have argued should have done more to limit the sale of advanced chips to China.
Trump acknowledged that Bessent and Lutnick “have two different views” on how fast Commerce should have acted.
“They’re fine,” Trump said of the two Cabinet secretaries. “One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow up with China.”
For his part, Trump defended the decision to delay labeling Megaspeed a national security threat.
“Well, he might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have, if you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow-up with China,” Trump told CNN’s Alayna Treene.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it. And I’ll make a decision, but I understand very well both sides,” he added.
Trump also on Monday offered a vote of confidence to Huang, saying he “would not mind” if the former Nvidia CEO were reinstated atop the chipmaking firm.
“I would not mind that,” Trump told reporters. “I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than the other. But I would certainly not mind seeing that.”
The president’s support came amid reports that Huang was discussing the possibility of a comeback effort just days after resigning under pressure over revelations of extramarital affairs — including one with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. (A source familiar said Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Huang back.)
Trump — who called Huang a “legend” in the hours after he stepped down — has repeatedly praised him despite the longstanding national security concerns about Huang harbored by some senior officials in his administration.
This story has been updated with additional information.
Hadas Gold contributed to this report.
